title: Global diesel crunch sends cost pressures down the supply chain
gist: Oxford Economics shows record US and European diesel prices (doubled since the war began) hit transport, agriculture and mining directly and spread via freight costs, with margin squeezes where pass-through is limited; domestic crude or refining cushions supply, not price.

insights.claim: US and European diesel prices hit record highs in mid-September and Asian prices rose sharply, with diesel prices roughly doubled since the war began.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Diesel cost pressure is a broad inflation and margin risk.

insights.claim: Direct diesel exposure is concentrated in land and water transport, mining and agriculture, and varies widely by country: India's land transport uses about 478 ktoe of diesel per $bn of real output versus 170 in the US and 240 in the EU.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: India and the EU are more exposed than the US; sector selection matters.

insights.claim: Diesel costs spread beyond direct users through freight rates; heavy, frequently transported goods and food manufacturers are most exposed via the indirect channel, and US trucking operating costs and freight producer prices are already rising.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Expect goods price pressure from freight pass-through.

insights.claim: The largest margin squeeze is likely where high exposure coincides with fixed-price contracts, weak demand or competition, so construction and farmers (limited pricing power) are more vulnerable than trucking, which can use fuel surcharges.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Short fixed-price contractors and farm producers over fuel-surcharge carriers on margin risk.

insights.claim: Crude and refined products trade in integrated global markets, so domestic crude output or refining (Saudi Arabia, Canada, US) reduces physical shortage risk but cannot insulate domestic businesses from global price shocks.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Distinguish physical supply vulnerability from price exposure when assessing countries.

insights.claim: India sharply raised duties on diesel exports to keep domestically refined barrels at home, while refining exporters like the Netherlands, South Korea and India remain exposed to higher feedstock costs.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Export curbs can tighten global diesel markets further.
